claim: The Dpp morphogen gradient is derived from the anterior stripe of cells in the Drosophila wing disc.
source: The Dpp morphogen gradient derived from the anterior stripe of cells is thought to control growth and patterning of the Drosophila wing disc.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field, referenced in the abstract as a foundational concept.

claim: The Dpp morphogen gradient is thought to control growth and patterning of the Drosophila wing disc.
source: The Dpp morphogen gradient derived from the anterior stripe of cells is thought to control growth and patterning of the Drosophila wing disc.
evidence: This represents established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: The spatial-temporal requirement of dpp for growth and patterning remained largely unknown.
source: However, the spatial-temporal requirement of dpp for growth and patterning remained largely unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to recent studies.

claim: Akiyama and Gibson (2015) proposed that the dpp stripe is critical for patterning but not for growth.
source: By generating a conditional null allele, one study proposed that the dpp stripe is critical for patterning but not for growth (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Akiyama and Gibson 2015 study.

claim: Akiyama and Gibson (2015) generated a conditional null allele of dpp.
source: By generating a conditional null allele, one study proposed that the dpp stripe is critical for patterning but not for growth (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Akiyama and Gibson 2015 study.

claim: Harmansa et al. (2015) used a membrane-anchored nanobody to trap Dpp.
source: In contrast, using a membrane-anchored nanobody to trap Dpp, the other study proposed that Dpp dispersal from the stripe is required for patterning and also for medial wing disc growth, at least in the posterior compartment (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Harmansa et al. 2015 study.

claim: Harmansa et al. (2015) proposed that Dpp dispersal from the stripe is required for patterning and medial wing disc growth in the posterior compartment.
source: In contrast, using a membrane-anchored nanobody to trap Dpp, the other study proposed that Dpp dispersal from the stripe is required for patterning and also for medial wing disc growth, at least in the posterior compartment (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Harmansa et al. 2015 study.

claim: Growth control by the Dpp morphogen gradient remains under debate.
source: Thus, growth control by the Dpp morphogen gradient remains under debate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conflicting findings from the two cited studies.

claim: The dpp stripe source is required for wing disc growth during third instar larval stages.
source: Here, by removing dpp from the stripe at different time points, we show that the dpp stripe source is indeed required for wing disc growth, also during third instar larval stages.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Morphogens are thought to disperse and form concentration gradients to control tissue patterning and growth.
source: Morphogens are thought to disperse and form concentration gradients to control tissue patterning and growth (Rogers and Schier, 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The Drosophila wing imaginal disc has served as an excellent model to study how morphogens control patterning and growth.
source: The Drosophila wing imaginal disc has served as an excellent model to study how morphogens control patterning and growth.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: dpp is a homologue of vertebrate bone morphogenetic protein 2/4 (BMP2/4).
source: It has been shown that decapentagplegic (dpp), a homologue of vertebrate bone morphogenetic protein 2/4 (BMP2/4), is expressed in a stripe of cells in the anterior compartment along the anterior-posterior compartmental boundary of the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: dpp is expressed in a stripe of cells in the anterior compartment along the anterior-posterior compartmental boundary of the wing imaginal disc.
source: It has been shown that decapentagplegic (dpp), a homologue of vertebrate bone morphogenetic protein 2/4 (BMP2/4), is expressed in a stripe of cells in the anterior compartment along the anterior-posterior compartmental boundary of the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Dpp protein is thought to spread from the stripe source and form a concentration gradient to control patterning and growth of the wing imaginal disc.
source: From this source, Dpp protein is thought to spread and form a concentration gradient to control patterning and growth of the wing imaginal disc (Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996; Matsuda et al., 2016; Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The precise spatial-temporal requirement of dpp remained elusive due to the inability to generate an inducible null allele.
source: However, the precise spatial-temporal requirement of dpp remained elusive, mainly because it was not possible to generate an inducible null allele of dpp due to the haploinsufficiency of the locus and the lack of appropriate methods.
evidence: This is an inference about the state of the field prior to recent technical advances.

claim: dpp exhibits haploinsufficiency.
source: However, the precise spatial-temporal requirement of dpp remained elusive, mainly because it was not possible to generate an inducible null allele of dpp due to the haploinsufficiency of the locus and the lack of appropriate methods.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the dpp locus.

claim: Akiyama and Gibson used CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome engineering to insert a FRT cassette into the dpp locus.
source: Akiyama and Gibson used CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome engineering techniques to insert a FRT (Flippase Recognition Target) cassette into the dpp locus, and successfully generated a conditional null allele of dpp using the expression of Flippase (FLP) in a spatial-temporal controlled manner (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Akiyama and Gibson 2015 study.

claim: Akiyama and Gibson successfully generated a conditional null allele of dpp using FLP expression in a spatial-temporal controlled manner.
source: Akiyama and Gibson used CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome engineering techniques to insert a FRT (Flippase Recognition Target) cassette into the dpp locus, and successfully generated a conditional null allele of dpp using the expression of Flippase (FLP) in a spatial-temporal controlled manner (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Akiyama and Gibson 2015 study.

claim: Akiyama and Gibson showed that the Dpp morphogen gradient derived from the anterior stripe is critical for patterning.
source: By genetically removing dpp from the anterior stripe, they showed that the Dpp morphogen gradient derived from this stripe is indeed critical for patterning.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Akiyama and Gibson 2015 study.

claim: Akiyama and Gibson found that dpp from the stripe is largely dispensable for wing disc growth during the third instar larval stage.
source: However, and rather surprisingly, they also found that dpp from the stripe is largely dispensable for wing disc growth during the third instar larval stage.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Akiyama and Gibson 2015 study.

claim: Growth of the wing disc was compromised by genetically removing dpp from the entire anterior compartment.
source: Instead, growth of the wing disc was compromised by genetically removing dpp from the entire anterior compartment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Akiyama and Gibson 2015 study.

claim: Akiyama and Gibson proposed that a not-yet identified anterior dpp source outside the stripe of cells is required for wing disc growth.
source: Based on the constant requirement of dpp derived from the anterior compartment for growth of the wing disc, Akiyama and Gibson proposed that a not-yet identified anterior dpp source outside the stripe of cells is required for wing disc growth (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Akiyama and Gibson 2015 study.

claim: Harmansa et al. used a membrane-anchored anti-GFP nanobody (morphotrap) to trap GFP-Dpp and manipulate GFP-Dpp dispersal.
source: Harmansa et al. used a membrane-anchored anti-GFP nanobody (morphotrap) to trap GFP-Dpp and manipulate GFP-Dpp dispersal (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Harmansa et al. 2015 study.

claim: An endogenously tagged GFP-Dpp strain was not available for the Harmansa et al. study.
source: Since an endogenously tagged GFP-Dpp strain was not available, dpp disc mutants were rescued by expressing GFP-Dpp in the stripe (Entchev et al., 2000; Teleman and Cohen, 2000) and morphotrap was concomitantly expressed in the stripe in order to trap GFP-Dpp and block its dispersal.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental setup used in the Harmansa et al. study.

claim: Harmansa et al. rescued dpp disc mutants by expressing GFP-Dpp in the stripe.
source: Since an endogenously tagged GFP-Dpp strain was not available, dpp disc mutants were rescued by expressing GFP-Dpp in the stripe (Entchev et al., 2000; Teleman and Cohen, 2000) and morphotrap was concomitantly expressed in the stripe in order to trap GFP-Dpp and block its dispersal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Entchev et al. 2000 and Teleman and Cohen 2000.

claim: Harmansa et al. confirmed that dpp is required for wing disc patterning.
source: In this setup, the authors confirmed that dpp is required for wing disc patterning, and also found that Dpp morphogen dispersal from the stripe of cells is required for medial but not for lateral wing disc growth in the posterior compartment (the region they analyzed).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Harmansa et al. 2015 study.

claim: Harmansa et al. found that Dpp morphogen dispersal from the stripe is required for medial but not for lateral wing disc growth in the posterior compartment.
source: In this setup, the authors confirmed that dpp is required for wing disc patterning, and also found that Dpp morphogen dispersal from the stripe of cells is required for medial but not for lateral wing disc growth in the posterior compartment (the region they analyzed).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Harmansa et al. 2015 study.

claim: The Harmansa et al. experiments were done under rescue conditions, potentially missing other dpp sources important for growth in wild type individuals.
source: However, since these experiments were done under rescue conditions, other sources of dpp important for growth in wild type individuals could have been missed.
evidence: This is an inference about potential limitations of the Harmansa et al. experimental approach.

claim: Both the Akiyama and Gibson study and the Harmansa et al. study confirmed a role of dpp on wing disc patterning.
source: Thus, while both studies confirmed a role of dpp on wing disc patterning, these studies propose different scenarios for the spatial requirement of dpp on wing disc growth, and it remains debated whether the Dpp morphogen gradient derived from the anterior stripe of cells is required for wing disc growth (Vincent et al., 2016; Strzyz, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings from both cited studies.

claim: It remains debated whether the Dpp morphogen gradient derived from the anterior stripe of cells is required for wing disc growth.
source: Thus, while both studies confirmed a role of dpp on wing disc patterning, these studies propose different scenarios for the spatial requirement of dpp on wing disc growth, and it remains debated whether the Dpp morphogen gradient derived from the anterior stripe of cells is required for wing disc growth (Vincent et al., 2016; Strzyz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vincent et al. 2016 and Strzyz 2016.

claim: The dpp-Gal4 driver line used by Akiyama and Gibson does not faithfully reflect the endogenous dpp expression pattern during third instar larval stages.
source: In this study, we first show that the dpp-Gal4 driver line used to remove dpp from the anterior stripe in the previous study (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015) does not faithfully reflect the endogenous dpp expression pattern during third instar larval stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: dpp from the stripe of cells is critical for growth of the wing disc, even during third instar larval stages.
source: Using this setup, we demonstrate that dpp from the stripe of cells is indeed critical for growth of the wing disc, even during third instar larval stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data.

claim: An anterior dpp source outside the stripe of cells, even if it exists, would not be sufficient to drive growth of the wing disc.
source: Furthermore, this result indicates that an anterior dpp source outside the stripe of cells, even if it would exist, would not be sufficient to drive growth of the wing disc.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings of the current study.

claim: Using dpp-Gal4 to remove dpp has intrinsic problems in removing dpp from the early onset of its expression.
source: Although it appears straightforward to use dpp-Gal4 to remove dpp, this setup has intrinsic problems in removing dpp from the early onset of its expression.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the dpp-Gal4 experimental approach.

claim: The dpp-Gal4 setup requires the dpp disc enhancer to be activated, meaning endogenous dpp is initially expressed before it can be removed by FLP/FRT recombination.
source: Since this setup requires the dpp disc enhancer to be activated, endogenous dpp is initially expressed before it can be removed by FLP/FRT recombination.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of the dpp-Gal4 system.

claim: It takes about 18–24 hr to remove the engineered cassette in the dpp locus from the majority of cells in the anterior stripe.
source: Furthermore, since it takes about 18–24 hr to remove the engineered cassette in the dpp locus from the majority of cells in the anterior stripe and the wing disc grows dramatically during this time (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015) (Figure 1a), this delay may fail to reveal a potential early function of dpp on growth.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Akiyama and Gibson 2015 and data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The wing disc grows dramatically during the 18-24 hr period required for cassette removal.
source: Furthermore, since it takes about 18–24 hr to remove the engineered cassette in the dpp locus from the majority of cells in the anterior stripe and the wing disc grows dramatically during this time (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015) (Figure 1a), this delay may fail to reveal a potential early function of dpp on growth.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Akiyama and Gibson 2015 and data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The delay in cassette removal may fail to reveal a potential early function of dpp on growth.
source: Furthermore, since it takes about 18–24 hr to remove the engineered cassette in the dpp locus from the majority of cells in the anterior stripe and the wing disc grows dramatically during this time (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015) (Figure 1a), this delay may fail to reveal a potential early function of dpp on growth.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: dpp has been shown to be expressed in the entire anterior stripe of cells from the early third instar larval stages.
source: Although dpp has been shown to be expressed in the entire anterior stripe of cells from the early third instar larval stages (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015), NLS-mCherry expressed under the control of dpp-Gal4 marked only the dorsal stripe of cells at the beginning of third instar larval stages (60 hr after egg laying (AEL) at 26°C) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Akiyama and Gibson 2015.

claim: NLS-mCherry expressed under the control of dpp-Gal4 marked only the dorsal stripe of cells at the beginning of third instar larval stages (60 hr AEL at 26°C).
source: Although dpp has been shown to be expressed in the entire anterior stripe of cells from the early third instar larval stages (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015), NLS-mCherry expressed under the control of dpp-Gal4 marked only the dorsal stripe of cells at the beginning of third instar larval stages (60 hr after egg laying (AEL) at 26°C) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: dpp-Gal4 was expressed in the entire stripe of cells only in relatively late third instar stages.
source: dpp-Gal4 was expressed in the entire stripe of cells only in relatively late third instar stages (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The fragment of the dpp disc enhancer used to drive Gal4 does not cover all the cis-regulatory regions important for proper stripe expression.
source: Most probably, the fragment of the dpp disc enhancer used to drive Gal4 does not cover all the cis-regulatory regions important for proper stripe expression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed expression pattern discrepancy.

claim: ptc is a Hedgehog target gene expressed in a stripe of cells similar to dpp.
source: Since ptc, a Hedgehog target gene, is expressed in a stripe of cells similar to dpp, we first analyzed the spatial-temporal expression pattern of ptc-Gal4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ptc expression.

claim: NLS-mCherry expressed under the control of ptc-Gal4 marked the entire stripe of cells as early as late second instar (50 hr AEL at 26°C).
source: We found that NLS-mCherry expressed under the control of ptc-Gal4 marked the entire stripe of cells as early as late second instar (50 hr AEL at 26°C) and that stripe expression continued throughout third instar larval stages (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: ptc-Gal4 stripe expression continued throughout third instar larval stages.
source: We found that NLS-mCherry expressed under the control of ptc-Gal4 marked the entire stripe of cells as early as late second instar (50 hr AEL at 26°C) and that stripe expression continued throughout third instar larval stages (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: dpp-Gal4 expression did not cover the ventral Dpp stripe in the early third instar larval stages.
source: Consistent with the above observations, dpp-Gal4 expression did not cover the ventral Dpp stripe in the early third instar larval stages and covered the entire stripe only in late third instar larval stages (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: dpp-Gal4 expression covered the entire Dpp stripe only in late third instar larval stages.
source: Consistent with the above observations, dpp-Gal4 expression did not cover the ventral Dpp stripe in the early third instar larval stages and covered the entire stripe only in late third instar larval stages (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: ptc-Gal4 expression continuously covered the Dpp stripe from the early third instar larval stages onward.
source: In contrast, ptc-Gal4 expression continuously covered the Dpp stripe from the early third instar larval stages onward (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: Fluorescent signal and antibody signal for mCherry overlap well.
source: To ascertain the validity of using NLS-mCherry to mark ptc-Gal4 or dpp-Gal4 expression, which might be somewhat compromised due to the lengthy maturation time for the mCherry protein, we marked Gal4 expression using α-mCherry antibody and found that fluorescent signal and antibody signal overlap well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spatial-temporal ptc-Gal4 expression reflects endogenous dpp expression pattern in the wing disc more precisely than dpp-Gal4.
source: Taken together, these results show that spatial-temporal ptc-Gal4 expression reflects endogenous dpp expression pattern in the wing disc more precisely than dpp-Gal4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative expression data presented.

claim: When dpp was removed using dpp-Gal4, pMad was not detectable in the wing pouch but the wing disc grew normally.
source: When dpp was removed using dpp-Gal4, pMad was not detectable in the wing pouch but the wing disc grew normally, as reported in Akiyama and Gibson (Figure 2a,b) (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,b and citation to Akiyama and Gibson 2015.

claim: When dpp was removed using ptc-Gal4, the pMad signal was lost from the wing pouch (except for the future alula region), and wing disc growth was severely affected.
source: In sharp contrast, when dpp was removed using ptc-Gal4, the pMad signal was also lost from the wing pouch (except for the future alula region), and wing disc growth was severely affected (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Wing pouches were very small and often hardly visible when dpp was removed using ptc-Gal4, as shown by the lack of internal ring expression of Wg.
source: Wing pouches were very small and often hardly visible, as shown by the lack of internal ring expression of Wg (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Dpp expression was lost from the stripe of anterior cells but remained detectable in the future alular region when dpp was removed using ptc-Gal4.
source: We confirmed that Dpp expression was lost from the stripe of anterior cells but remained detectable in the future alular region (Figure 2d), consistent with the pMad signal in this region (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2d and 2c.

claim: The growth repressor Brk, normally repressed by pMad, was uniformly expressed in the wing pouch when dpp was removed using ptc-Gal4.
source: Accordingly, the growth repressor Brk, normally repressed by pMad, was uniformly expressed in the wing pouch (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Wing disc growth is severely affected by removing dpp using ptc-Gal4.
source: The above results show that wing disc growth is severely affected by removing dpp using ptc-gal4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: When one copy of dpp was removed using ptc-Gal4 (control), the entire anterior wing pouch was marked in some wing discs, and only a stripe of anterior cells was marked in other wing discs.
source: We found that when one copy of dpp was removed using ptc-Gal4 (control), the entire anterior wing pouch was marked in some wing discs, and only a stripe of anterior cells was marked in other wing discs (Figure 2f,g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2f,g.

claim: Similar cell lineages were observed when two copies of dpp were removed using ptc-Gal4.
source: Similar cell lineages were also observed when two copies of dpp were removed using ptc-Gal4 (Figure 2h,i).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2h,i.

claim: The variations in ptc-Gal4 lineages observed may be due to slight differences in Gal4 or FLP expression or a degree of randomness in the excision events in each wing disc.
source: The variations in these ptc-Gal4 lineages observed may be due to slight differences in Gal4 or FLP expression or a degree of randomness in the excision events in each wing disc.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of observed variability.

claim: The wing discs where the ptc-Gal4 lineages were restricted to a stripe of cells showed drastic growth defects.
source: Importantly, the wing discs where the ptc-Gal4 lineages were restricted to a stripe of cells showed drastic growth defects (Figure 2i), raising a possibility that dpp derived from the anterior stripe is critical for wing disc growth.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: dpp derived from the anterior stripe is critical for wing disc growth.
source: Importantly, the wing discs where the ptc-Gal4 lineages were restricted to a stripe of cells showed drastic growth defects (Figure 2i), raising a possibility that dpp derived from the anterior stripe is critical for wing disc growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The severe growth defects by ptc-Gal4 may simply reflect an early role of dpp stripe on wing disc growth.
source: However, since ptc-Gal4 is expressed earlier than dpp-Gal4 (Figure 1), the severe growth defects by ptc-Gal4 may simply reflect an early role of dpp stripe on wing disc growth.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative explanations for the observed phenotype.

claim: Different FRT cassettes can have different sensitivities to FLPase.
source: Furthermore, since different FRT cassettes can have different sensitivities to FLPase, the FRT cassette in dpp locus and the FRT cassette to follow the ptc-Gal4 lineage could be excised in different regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FRT/FLP systems.

claim: Gal80ts represses Gal4 activity at 17°C and can be inactivated at 29°C.
source: Gal80ts represses Gal4 activity at 17°C and can be inactivated at 29°C.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Gal80ts system.

claim: ptc-Gal4 can be conditionally activated upon a temperature shift using the Gal80ts system.
source: Thus, ptc-Gal4 can be conditionally activated upon a temperature shift.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the Gal80ts system.

claim: At the permissive temperature, dppFO, ptc-Gal4 / dppFO; tub-Gal80ts / UAS-FLP adult wing had no obvious wing phenotype.
source: Indeed, we found that at the permissive temperature dppFO, ptc-Gal4 / dppFO; tub-Gal80ts / UAS-FLP adult wing had no obvious wing phenotype, suggesting that Gal80ts effectively suppresses ptc-Gal4 activity at 17°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gal80ts effectively suppresses ptc-Gal4 activity at 17°C.
source: Indeed, we found that at the permissive temperature dppFO, ptc-Gal4 / dppFO; tub-Gal80ts / UAS-FLP adult wing had no obvious wing phenotype, suggesting that Gal80ts effectively suppresses ptc-Gal4 activity at 17°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of wing phenotype at permissive temperature.

claim: ptc-Gal4 lineages were strictly restricted to the anterior stripe in control and mutant wing disc when FLP/FRT-mediated recombination was temporally activated at the beginning of the second or third instar larval stage using Gal80ts.
source: We first marked lineages of ptc-Gal4 when FLP/FRT-mediated recombination was temporally activated at the beginning of the second or third instar larval stage using Gal80ts. We found that ptc-Gal4 lineages were strictly restricted to the anterior stripe in control and mutant wing disc (Figure 3b,d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3b,d.

claim: The more random lineages shown in Figure 2g,i appear to be derived from early expression of the ptc-Gal4 driver.
source: Thus, the more random lineages shown in Figure 2g,i appear to be derived from early expression of the ptc-Gal4 driver.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of lineage patterns with and without temporal control.

claim: FLP/FRT-mediated excision in the dpp locus was restricted to the anterior stripe from second and from third instar larval stages, although the excision varied within the stripe.
source: Using this setup, we found that FLP/FRT-mediated excision in the dpp locus was indeed restricted to the anterior stripe from second and from third instar larval stages although the excision varied within the stripe (21/21 and 14/14 wing discs, respectively) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The temporal lineages of ptc-Gal4 reflect the actual region where dpp is removed.
source: This result also strongly suggests that the temporal lineages of ptc-Gal4 indeed reflect the actual region where dpp is removed in this setup (Figure 3b,d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the dppFO-GFP lineage tracing data.

claim: Wing disc growth was severely affected when dpp was removed during either second or third instar larval stages, as measured in the late third instar larval stages.
source: By removing dpp during either second or third instar larval stages, we found that wing disc growth was severely affected in both cases, as measured in the late third instar larval stages (53 hr or 43 hr later after temperature shift, respectively) (Figure 3b'–e').
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3b'–e'.

claim: The majority of Dpp was eliminated around 20 ~ 24 hr after temperature shift.
source: The majority of Dpp was eliminated around 20 ~ 24 hr after temperature shift as also reported by Akiyama and Gibson (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and wing disc appeared to grow at least until 24 hr after temperature shift.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and citation to Akiyama and Gibson 2015.

claim: Wing disc appeared to grow at least until 24 hr after temperature shift.
source: The majority of Dpp was eliminated around 20 ~ 24 hr after temperature shift as also reported by Akiyama and Gibson (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and wing disc appeared to grow at least until 24 hr after temperature shift.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data.

claim: The growth defects resulting from temperature shifting at the beginning of third instar larval stages likely reflect the effects seen from the absence of dpp around mid-third instar larval stages.
source: Thus, the growth defects resulting from temperature shifting at the beginning of third instar larval stages likely reflect the effects seen from the absence of dpp around mid-third instar larval stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of Dpp elimination and growth observation.

claim: The dpp stripe is required for wing disc growth during second and even third instar larval stages.
source: These results show that the dpp stripe is required for wing disc growth during second and even third instar larval stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from temporal dpp removal.

claim: The different growth defects observed should be due to the differences between the dpp-Gal4 and ptc-Gal4 driver lines.
source: Since we used the same dpp allele (dppFO) and UAS-FLP line as Akiyama and Gibson, the different growth defects observed should be due to the differences between the dpp-Gal4 and ptc-Gal4 driver lines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The differences in the spatial-temporal expression may be responsible for the different phenotype observed when using dpp-Gal4 or ptc-Gal4.
source: We showed that while ptc-Gal4 is constantly expressed at the anterior stripe during third instar larval stages, dpp-Gal4 is initially expressed only at the dorsal stripe and only later, during third instar larval stages, in the entire stripe (Figure 1). Thus, the differences in the spatial-temporal expression may be responsible for the different phenotype observed when using dpp-Gal4 or ptc-Gal4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern comparison.

claim: At the mid third instar larval stage (80 hrAEL at 26°C), Brk was repressed in the ventral compartment where dpp was still expressed but was slightly upregulated in the dorsal compartment where the majority of dpp was removed.
source: We found that at the mid third instar larval stage (80 hrAEL at 26°C), Brk was repressed in the ventral compartment where dpp was still expressed but was slightly upregulated in the dorsal compartment where the majority of dpp was removed (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Brk upregulation in the dorsal compartment was not uniform but graded; lower in ventral and higher in dorsal regions within the dorsal compartment.
source: Interestingly, Brk upregulation in the dorsal compartment was not uniform but graded; lower in ventral and higher in dorsal regions within the dorsal compartment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: At the late third instar larval stage, the majority of dpp was eliminated and Brk was upregulated in both dorsal and ventral compartment but Brk was not uniformly upregulated.
source: At the late third instar larval stage, the majority of dpp was eliminated and Brk was upregulated in both dorsal and ventral compartment but again, Brk was not uniformly upregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Omb has been shown to be weakly expressed when dpp is removed using dpp-Gal4.
source: Consistent with our findings, Omb has been shown to be weakly expressed in this setup (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Akiyama and Gibson 2015.

claim: The Dpp signal is not completely removed from the wing imaginal disc when using dpp-Gal4.
source: These results suggest that the Dpp signal is not completely removed from the wing imaginal disc when using dpp-Gal4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Brk expression pattern data.

claim: The graded Brk expression in the dorsal compartment is consistent with weak Dpp signal derived from the ventral dpp stripe.
source: The graded Brk expression in the dorsal compartment is consistent with weak Dpp signal derived from the ventral dpp stripe, and this lasting signal can explain the sustained growth there with minor growth defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Brk expression pattern.

claim: When dpp was removed by ptc-Gal4 during the third instar larval stages, majority of dpp was removed from the entire anterior stripe.
source: In contrast, when dpp was removed by ptc-Gal4 during the third instar larval stages, majority of dpp was removed from the entire anterior stripe (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and wing disc growth was severely affected (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The critical role of the dpp stripe on wing disc growth was missed by Akiyama and Gibson due to imprecise spatial removal of dpp when using dpp-Gal4 during third instar larval stages.
source: Together, these results suggest that the critical role of the dpp stripe on wing disc growth was missed by Akiyama and Gibson due to imprecise spatial removal of dpp when using dpp-Gal4 during third instar larval stages (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative experimental results.

claim: The strong growth defects resulting from removing dpp from the entire anterior compartment are most likely due to excision of dpp from the anterior stripe and not due to the excision of the potential dpp outside the stripe.
source: However, our data show that wing disc growth was severely affected when dpp was removed only from the anterior stripe during third instar larval stages. Thus, the strong growth defects resulting from removing dpp from the entire anterior compartment are most likely due to excision of dpp from the anterior stripe and not due to the excision of the potential dpp outside the stripe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The anterior dpp stripe is critical for growth as well as patterning of the wing imaginal disc.
source: In conclusion, our results establish that the anterior dpp stripe is critical for growth as well as patterning of the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: It remains an open question whether the requirement of the dpp stripe on wing disc growth changes over time.
source: Given the slow process of removing dpp by FLP/FRT mediated recombination (about 20–24 hr) compared to wing disc growth, it remains an open question whether the requirement of the dpp stripe on wing disc growth changes over time.
evidence: This is speculation about limitations and future directions.

claim: It would be important to acutely manipulate the endogenous morphogen gradient at the protein level to address the precise temporal requirement of the dpp stripe on wing disc growth.
source: It would be important to acutely manipulate the endogenous morphogen gradient at the protein level to address the precise temporal requirement of the dpp stripe on wing disc growth (Matsuda et al., 2016; Bieli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research, supported by citations to relevant methodological papers.
